# The skill writer's standing brief

You are the writer for the project skills of the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. The skills are under `.claude/skills/`.

The coordinating session briefs you. It resumes this session for each writing task. Keep this brief in mind after a task ends. You are not the coordinating session: do not follow the boot order in `CLAUDE.md`, and do not read `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` or `INDEX.md` unless a task names an entry.

The curator is the person who directs this restoration. The curator reads the skills on a phone, cold, without the project's records in mind. Every agent that works in the repository reads them in the same way.

# Your standing order

These rules hold for every task.

## 1. Write in ASD-STE100, at least halfway

ASD-STE100 is Simplified Technical English. It has two kinds of text, and you need both:

- **Descriptive text** says what a thing is and how it works. Give the most important information first. Write one topic in each paragraph. Keep each sentence to 25 words or fewer.
- **Procedural text** gives steps. Write one instruction in each sentence. Put the condition first: "If X, do Y." Use the imperative. Keep each sentence to 20 words or fewer.

Describe first, then give the procedure. A procedure without a description underneath reads like if/else code, and the reader cannot hold it in mind.

More rules:

- Define a term before you use it. After that, use the same word for the same thing every time. Do not use two words for one thing, or one word for two things.
- Define a term in the skill's glossary only if it recurs with one meaning. Elsewhere, write plain words.
- Say what to do. Use "do not" only where no positive instruction says the same thing.
- Do not fold a list into a sentence. Use a vertical list.
- Keep the small words: "the", "a", "that". Do not write in telegraphic shorthand.
- Do not write a rule that changes nothing, such as a rule to follow the brief.
- A rewrite of existing text is never longer than the text it replaces. New content that a task asks for may add length, unless the part has a budget, as the orientation (`fortress-repo`'s revival part) has. There, new content competes for space with the text already there.

Example. Bad: "Name the way that changes nothing." Good: "Tell which solution keeps the current behaviour."

## 2. The glossary form

A skill's terms open the skill, in `SKILL.md`, as a definition list with no heading. Each term is bold on its own line. The definition follows on the next line, after ": ". It opens with a noun phrase. Write the term and that noun phrase as a dictionary does, with no article: "revival", not "the revival"; "Person in charge of this restoration", not "The person in charge". The curator chose this form. `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` is the model.

## 3. Do not take the register of what you read

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, the batch records and many notes were written by earlier models. They use dense agent shorthand: long sentences with many clauses, invented phrases, and terms that only make sense with the whole record in mind. Read them for their content only. Do not copy their wording or their style. Before you keep a sentence, ask: can a reader who is new to the repository understand this sentence without the record?

## 4. The principles

`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md` gives the seven principles by which the curator wants a skill written, each with its reason and a pair of texts: one he marked, and the one he accepted. Read it before your first edit. Apply it to every sentence that you write or keep.

## 5. How you work

- Edit the skill files in place. Git keeps the earlier text.
- A comment of the curator marks a problem area. Fix it at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote: `git add -- <paths> && git commit -m '<message>' -- <paths>`. End every commit message with these two lines, exactly:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

- Do not push. The coordinator pushes.
- Do not touch the review page or its scratch files. The coordinator keeps the page in step.
- Provenance goes only in the skill's `references/sources.md`: one line per change. Name its source exactly: the curator's comment and its date, a POSITIONS entry by its title, or "settled by the coordinator". Do not attribute to the curator a choice that the coordinator made.
- A part states each rule as the tree holds it. Name no question, item, batch, rung or record file as its source, and give no decision's status (who decided, answered, pending, default). When the curator answers a question, change a part only if the tree changes. In `sources.md`, write provenance as dated history, never as current status.
- Before each commit, run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` on the files you changed. Remove every hit, or say in your report why a hit is a rule.
- Do not change what a rule means unless the task asks for it. If a change of meaning seems right, do not make it. List it in your report as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
- Check a claim about the code against the code before you write it. If the task's reason for a change is wrong, say so in your report.
- Do not write a model identifier string anywhere. Name models by tier.
- Use `git grep`, not `grep -r`.

## 6. Your report

End each task with a report in plain short sentences:

- the commits, with their hashes;
- the new text of each changed sentence, or for a larger change, each file's size before and after and what changed;
- the decisions not taken, each with its alternatives;
- anything in the task that you could not follow, and why.

## P-37

Now:

> - P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library. The decision is not put to him again. How the checker comes to accept the library, its first step and the order of the work, was left to a plan for him, which he approved (P-33).

Evidence: explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/P-37.md; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/judgement-c2.md:144; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c2.md:199; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/takeaway-c2.md:129

## P-26

Now:

> - P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper (F-166). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.

Evidence: explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/P-26.md; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/judgement-c1.md:180; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md:260; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/takeaway-c1.md:154

## P-43

Now:

> - P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.

Evidence: explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/P-43.md; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/judgement-c3.md:60; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c3.md:82; explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/takeaway-c3.md:38

## P-158

Now:

> - P-158 **A member that an api writes `abstract` is declared in the component that exports the api.** The component's trait or object declares each such member at the api's header, with a body or without one. The compiled export check refuses a component that leaves one out, and the checker then checks that each object defines it. Why: the compiler's prelude, the team's later work, restates each such member in the component without a body, and the team's export check of 2012 enforces it; by P-26, on the team's later word, that way wins over the interpreter's library, written earlier for walk, which leaves some out. The specification asks for no body there, not for no declaration (`Specification/basic/components/apis.tex`, "Component and API Identity"). Without the declaration, a compiled client's call of the member dies with `NoSuchMethodError` (row 816).

1	<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->
2	
3	# Writing the skills
4	
5	The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.
6	
7	## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else
8	
9	A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
10	- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
11	- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."
12	
13	## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them
14	
15	A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
16	- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
17	- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."
18	
19	## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest
20	
21	Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
22	- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
23	- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"
24	
25	## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work
26	
27	A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
28	- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
29	- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."
30	
31	Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.
32	
33	## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name
34	
35	A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
36	- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
37	- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."
38	
39	## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace
40	
41	The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
42	- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
43	- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."
44	
45	Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.
46	
47	## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read
48	
49	A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
50	- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
51	- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

14:## What an entry is
15-
16-An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17-
18-- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19-- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20-- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
21-- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
22-- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
23-- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
24-- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
25-- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
26-- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
27-- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
28-- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
29-- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
30-- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
31-
32-Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
33-
34-1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
35-2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
36-3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
37-4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
38-5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
39-6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
40-
41-In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:
42-
43-- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
44-- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
45-- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
46-- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
47-- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
48-- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
49-
50-An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
51-
52-- keep: every check passes;
53-- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
54-- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;

264	On October 22 the curator supplied a screenshot and copied text of a proposed P-45 revision from the positions audit. The artifact URL could not be retrieved; this review concerns the supplied example, not the entire list. The screenshot distinguishes deletions from retained text; the copied text alone mixes both. The original ruling and its provenance have not been re-audited here.
265	
266	**Finding:** removing historical material improves the entry but does not by itself make the remaining decision understandable. The difficulty is visible in the formulation, not necessarily a lack of Fortress knowledge on the reader's part.
267	
268	- It mixes requirements with statements of implementation behaviour. “The checker runs” and “walk and the checker accept the same pairs” read as established facts, while “Still to build” points to remaining disagreements. State clearly whether agreement is a requirement or an achieved result.
269	- “No parameter pair required to exclude”, “refused families” and “reads otherwise” conceal important meaning in compressed technical wording. Name the objects and the operation precisely.
270	- “The paper's three overloading rules” neither identifies the paper precisely nor states enough of the decision to orient the reader. A reference may supply detail; it should not replace the explanation of what was decided.
271	- “No model line changes” compresses a consequential constraint into project shorthand. Identify the microGPT model program and state the exact restriction established by the ruling.
272	- A tracked diff makes historical and current wording compete for attention. Show the clean proposed entry first, with the diff available underneath.
273	
274	### Proposed form, subject to checking the ruling
275	
276	Lead with the decision. Follow with its essential scope, reason and exact technical conditions. Distinguish any remaining implementation work and point to its proper record. Preserve conditions that limit the decision; do not simplify away those conditions merely to improve fluency.
277	
278	An illustrative opening is:
279	
280	> **P-45 — Use the 2011 overloading model in the specification and both execution paths.** Allow overloads whose static parameters differ. The compiler's checker and the interpreter must apply the same rules when deciding which overload declarations are permitted.
281	
282	This is a presentation example, **not a verified replacement for P45**. It must be checked against the curator's actual ruling before adoption, and it does not replace the technical requirements omitted from this short opening. In the final entry, identify the 2011 source precisely. Do not turn an implementation default or a writer's inference into the curator's decision.
283	
284	### Two checks in the existing rewrite process
285	
286	1. **Fidelity:** compare the proposed entry with the recorded ruling and its qualifications. Distinguish the curator's words from the coordinator's interpretation, an implementation choice and a fact about the current tree. Keep the provenance in history.
287	2. **Comprehensibility:** give a cold reader the clean entry and its declared prerequisite context, without the original discussion. Ask it to paraphrase what the curator decided, where it applies, what it requires, and what remains unfinished. Compare that paraphrase with the source-backed meaning. If the reader has to reconstruct the original discussion to resolve the wording, revise the entry.
288	
289	The acceptance question is:
290	
291	> Can a reader distinguish what Pavol decided, what the implementation currently does, and what remains unfinished?
292	
293	A citation establishes where a statement came from; it does not establish that the statement communicates its meaning. This check does not require a type-theory lesson inside every position. It requires enough context to identify the decision before following pointers for technical detail.
294	
295	This is a proposed improvement to positions writing, distinct from Revival's admission rule. A ruling remains part of POSITIONS even when a worker would already agree with it by default. No POSITIONS entry, skill or audit proposal was edited here.

This section is the starting brief for that work; the rest of this report supplies background. It does not authorize changing a ruling or treating a proposed wording as an approved decision.

301	### Reader and register
302	
303	Assume the reader knows the relevant language concepts, or can reach their definitions through the normal skill references, but does not remember the conversation that produced the decision. A position must communicate the ruling without requiring that conversation.
304	
305	Apply the project's existing **ASD-STE100-inspired register (“halfway”)** to these entries, not only to skills. Read:
306	
307	- `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`, section 1, for the writing guidance.
308	- `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`, for the worked examples and principles.
309	- `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`, for entry ownership, scope, history and the record-writing procedure.
310	
311	These are writing references, not a request to adopt unrelated skill-writer duties. Use familiar verbs, explicit subjects and antecedents, consistent technical terms, and one main point per sentence. Put the condition before the action when that makes the rule easier to follow. Separate a decision from its reason and implementation status. Short sentences must preserve qualifications; do not meet a word target by replacing precise meaning with shorthand.
312	
313	The curator suspects that older entries predate this register and have not received a comparable prose pass. That chronology has not been established entry by entry. The observed wording defects justify the clarity pass regardless of their age. This is an adaptation of ASD-STE100 guidance, not a claim of formal compliance.
314	
315	### What the supplied examples show
316	
317	The P45, P50 and P51 reviews are based on the curator's pasted text and screenshots of proposed edits, not a fresh verification of the original rulings.
318	
319	**P45 needs structural clarification.** Separate what the curator requires from claims about achieved behaviour. Lead with the decision; retain exact technical restrictions; put detailed implementation gaps in their existing record homes, with a concise pointer where needed. The illustrative opening in the preceding P45 section remains provisional.
320	
321	**P50 and P51 need a smaller clarity pass.** Each already centres on a recognizable rule. Removing the historical material is useful; do not require a wholesale rewrite merely because the reader needs language knowledge.

325	- Replace the grammatical compression “its exits' with values” with wording that explicitly identifies the values supplied by exits.
326	- “P-51 is the other half of item 48” describes the old discussion's organization. State the substantive relationship if it helps the reader; otherwise leave that association in history.
327	- Expected-type propagation into the label body and its exits is the central decision. Keep its scope intact. Verify any proposed restatement against the ruling rather than inferring further type-theoretical claims from it.
328

331	- “When the checker's attempts at a call keep none” should identify exactly what the initial check failed to find. “If the initial check finds no applicable overload” is a possible wording **only if it matches the recorded trigger**.
332	- Distinguish the outer call from the inner call used as its argument. Repeated uses of “call” should not force the reader to infer which one is meant.
333	- Preserve the boundary “any inferred static argument, not only a result-only type parameter”. This affects which cases the decision covers.
334	- Replace “it makes the inference rules one rule everywhere” with the particular consistency the ruling sought. Do not widen the decision or invent a stronger rationale.
335	- The probe's measurement belongs in its report. A short implementation-status statement can remain if it accurately reports the relevant completion; it must not imply that every related gap is closed.

Revival retains its narrower role of correcting mistaken assumptions about revived Fortress. # The foundations of the revival: the judgement

## 0. How to read this

- **The three layers**, his frame of 2026-10-26 05:25 UTC. L1, the language: the Working Draft (WD, the team's text of 2010-12, copied 2011-02-02), the revised specification, the papers of 2011, 2012 and 2019, the 2012 restart's Types chapter, the team's library as a statement of the language, and the team's later published word. L2, the team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled path's checker, code generator, class loader and run time, the compiler's prelude, and walk. L3, Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer does not by itself decide a question in another. Where a team text in L1 itself argues from L2 or L3 (as the 2011 paper argues from Java), the text is the team's L1 word and its argument is theirs to make; I count it as L1.
- **Verdicts.** *Holds*: the tenet is right and its sound reason exists in the right layer. *Holds, text*: right, but its entry states a weaker, misplaced or wrong reason, or lacks the reason the coordinator needs to weigh a trade-off. *Bends*: against a team text where the team left a way the revival did not take. *Reverse*. None of the nine is a bend or a reversal.
- **Consequential** is the coordinator skill's test: reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of his; touches microGPT; chooses where the three principles split or are silent; or cannot be undone. A ruling so marked is his; each carries a default.
- **Earlier judgements**: J0929 (`decisions-review/judgement.md`), R0929 (`popl-recheck.md`), J1023 (`type-decisions-review/judgement.md`), J1024 (`phase3-exit/judgement.md`). I do not repeat their rulings; section 6 lists where this review's evidence changes one.

## 1. In short

1. **His doubt is answered: no foundational decision was a mistake.** All nine tenets hold. Three were taken on incomplete or partly wrong information (P-42, P-43, P-37), and in each case the missing or corrected fact makes the decision stronger or leaves it unchanged. None weakens it.
2. **The layers were mixed in the record's reasons, not in his decisions.** Four entries state a reason in the wrong layer or with the wrong date: P-26's list of "later word" counts 2009 prelude code as later than 2010-2012 texts; P-43's "Why" calls the prelude "the team's last record of the Fortress way"; P-37 lets the one library "take a design of the prelude's" with no rule for when; P-42 says "the switch-over ends the departure" where one line of `Shell.java` does. One judgement of 2026-09-20 read a WD sentence (L1) as the reason to keep a compiled-path setting (L2); P-42 corrected the language rule nine days later, and the code change is still owed. The rewrites fix the reasons; no decision turns.
3. **The bound.** P-42 holds on L1 grounds now stronger than when he decided: POPL 2019 says `Any` in so many words; the WD's `Object` sentence is not in the 2008 text, enters in a 2009 bulk import, and the same WD section says type parameters take tuple and arrow types; the library instantiates at tuples; the 2012 Types chapter and Welterweight put tuples and `()` outside `Object`. Steele's 2012 commits implemented the WD's sentence on the compiled path ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), found it broke walk's tests, and confined it to the compiled path by a setting, inserting `extends Any` wherever the compiled libraries and tests needed tuples, arrows or `()`. That is enforcement of a written sentence on one path, not a choice of the language's rule; the team's later texts (Types 2012, POPL 2019) do not carry `Object`. The probe shows the compiled run time needs nothing for the switch: under `Any` tuple and arrow static arguments compile, load and run as they do with `extends Any` written; under `Object` the compile command silently miscompiles `id((3, 4))` as `id(3)` (row 691). Java interoperability points the same way: `java.lang.Object` is Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`). The bound is not a linchpin: only one line of `Shell.java` and ten test files rest on it.
4. **The prelude question.** A design of the compiler's prelude binds the one library when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is silent or ambiguous and the team's own compiled checker enforces the design as a rule; a stub by the team's words, or an accommodation of a JVM or checker limit, does not bind; and "later" is a date, so a prelude line counts as later only if it is later than the library's text on the same shape and no later L1 text contradicts it. Under that rule the revival kept the interpreter library's text against a backed prelude design in exactly one place, row 816, reversed by P-158. The sweep's three dated designs do not bind: `fail(s: String): Zilch` (Steele 2011) is contradicted by the 2012 Types chapter and POPL 2019, which make `Bottom` inexpressible, and the revival's instance rule is POPL 2019's own; the order traits' `comprises T` (Steele 2012-06) spells a fact the checker now reads from the F-bound, and Naden's last word points to the bound-based form; `String`'s left-only concatenation has no team reason and the library's text and the specification's juxtaposition rule decide against it.
5. **Phase 3 closes with climb batch 22c**, which must carry four rungs: row 816's repair (P-158), row 782's nine operator headers with the export check reading operators (P-155 read to cover it), `List`'s two imports into the thirteen, and the bound `Any` for `fortress compile`. Its exit gate: the distance 0 over the thirteen, under the compile command's own setting, with operators and `abstract` read the team's way. Row 701, row 321, the 52 code-generator refusals and the natives are phase 4's. This moves the flip earlier than J1024 placed it.
6. **The rewrites** (section 5) are P-26, P-37, P-43, P-42, P-33, and smaller corrections to P-7, P-12, P-59, P-17/P-84, P-58. Each must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer, date "later" correctly, and know what the switch-over must run as well as check.

## 2. The nine tenets

### Tenet 1. The goal and its measure (P-7, P-8). Holds.

- **Sound reason and layer.** The goal joins two layers on purpose: the intent is judged in L1 (the specification as the revival revises it, the 2012 Types chapter beside it); the measure is L2 (microGPT compiled to JVM bytecode, running fast). The language itself states the aim: the WD is "designed for producing robust high-performance software" (`philosophy.tex:14-18`, `:33-35`). P-8 is a rule of weighing, his words, and lists "the implementations" among the designers' sources: right, so long as an implementation's word is read as L2 evidence.
- **Where the entry crosses layers.** P-7's second sentence, "where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work", is his 10-12 words and is the mechanism of P-26. "Later work in the compiler" is two things: a rule the team's checker enforces on purpose (L1 intent shown in L2 code) and an accommodation of the JVM or of a checker gap (L2 only). P-7 should not restate the rule; it should point to P-26, where the distinction lives (ruling 5).
- **Risk, not defect.** The team's wind-down named a conflict between the two halves (the type system against "a virtual machine not designed to support it"), and Steele's 2016 slide 45 proposed "a less complex type system". No measurement settles it for microGPT: no compiled kernel exists, no Java baseline is written. The tenet's two halves can pull apart at phase 5 and 6; that is the goal's own risk, known since 2026-09-08, and not a reason to change it.
- **Default:** stands. P-7's revision sentence points to P-26. Not consequential (a text edit the coordinator shows him).

### Tenet 2. The team's later word wins (P-26). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason, L1.** The WD contradicts itself (its types chapter: the numeric types "are mutually exclusive"; its library chapters: ℤ a subtype of ℚ) and was last edited 2010-12. The type group's texts of 2011 (OOPSLA), 2012 (Types chapter, Naden, Welterweight) and 2019 (POPL) are later and consistent on the exclusion rule, the three overloading rules and the default bound. Ranking later consistent texts above an earlier self-contradicting one is the right rule for this language, as J0929 F3 said.
- **Where the entry misstates.** (a) Its reason is an L2 motive: the type group "worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible". A JVM limit the team hit is evidence about L2, not a reason to rank an L1 text. (b) Its list of the later word mixes layers and dates: "the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010" is L2 code, earlier than the WD's last edit (2010-12), earlier than the 2011 paper, with no stated reason (`6896886fb` is a code-generator commit whose message ends "this would be a good time to get coercion working"). (c) "Specialization kept" names an L1 thing in P-26 (an overload for one instantiation, chosen at run time) and an L2 thing in the skill's `exploring.md:20` (a class per instantiation). (d) "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text" is the coordinator's sentence with no source (rq 215). (e) P-26 has been applied with L2 code as the later word in P-43's "Why", P-153 ("the team's later code") and P-158's reason. Of these, P-158 is sound for another reason (ruling 3); P-43's and P-153's conclusions are sound on L1 grounds the entries do not name.
- **The limit the exclusion brief named** stands: where two of the team's later sources conflict (the interpreter's nested library kept to 2012 against the prelude flat since 2009; the 2012 patents' forest rule against POPL 2019), P-26 gives no order, and P-8 decides by the goal. That is how route A was chosen and it is the right order of the two rules.
- **Default:** stands; rewritten to state the layer rule and the dating rule (section 5). Strike the "unfinished text" sentence (rq 215; nothing rests on it). Consequential in that it narrows what counts as "later word": his, and he said yes to the rewording on 10-26 07:42 UTC; the text passes the trap test before it enters.

### Tenet 3. One library, the interpreter's (P-37). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason, L1.** The specification knows one default library, "chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`" (`library/structure.tex:15-20`), and never names the compiler's. The interpreter's library is the team's statement of the language's library. The prelude is a bootstrap by the team's own words: "stripped-down minimalist ... first crack at compilation" (2008), "bogus" (2009), "bogo-trait" (2012), "Hopefully temporary hack" (`WellKnownNames.java:113-116`). The split's stated reason is L3, "importing java objects cleanly", and P-58 answers that reason. His goal of 10-26 ("avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library; continue the type checker so that it accepts the fuller library") is the L1 reason and is not in the entry.
- **The premise, and what measured it.** The decision assumes the compiled path can run the library, not only check it. Measured: code generation per declaration refuses 52 declarations of the twelve that the checker passes (F-34); tuple and arrow static arguments run on the class loader, `()` dies (row 339), a generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter dies (new, no row). Not measured: any library jar loaded and run compiled. So the premise is unmeasured, not refuted. His own doubt of 2026-09-20 15:18 UTC ("it tells you nothing of how much work is to get the interpreter running with the compiler") was recorded as not answered; F-34 and J1024's two phase-4 zeros are now the answer, and the entry should carry it.
- **Where the entry crosses layers.** "The one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types": this reads an L2 bootstrap as a design source with no rule for when. The ruling he received on 09-20 called the prelude "a record of what they could do behind the JVM wall" (L2); P-43's "Why" calls the same prelude "the team's last record of the Fortress way" (L1). Ruling 3 gives the rule that resolves the two.
- **Default:** stands. The rewrite adds his reason of 10-26, states that the switch-over needs the library to compile and run as well as check (phase 4's second zero), and carries ruling 3's rule for prelude designs. His (he approved the rewording).

### Tenet 4. The implicit bound `Any` (P-42). Holds, text. Ruling 4 gives the detail.

- **Default:** stands, grounds restated; "functions" dropped (rq 218; the specification's own callout already says "tuples and `()`"); the flip of `Shell.java:372` lands in 22c. His entry; the flip is a code change the entry already promises.

### Tenet 5. The exclusion rule and the flat number types (P-43). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason, L1.** The exclusion rule is the type group's published position four times over: the 2011 paper (`exclusion.tick:141-152`), the 2012 Types chapter (`types.tick:355-376`), Naden's "blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`), POPL 2019's [Anc-Same-Trait]. Under the rule a nested tower whose every level carries the self-typed algebra traits at its own type is impossible: one `ZZ32` would be `Equality` at five instantiations. The WD's own types chapter says the numeric types "are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`), kept word for word in 2012. Steele's 2016 talk draws the tower flat. Route C, the patents' forest rule, was built as a shadow and priced (F-46): its soundness rule is the revival's, not the team's, and it needs code-generator, walk and checker work the team never did. The 2011 paper's own argument for the rule cites Java ("it is already required in Java") and decidability; that is the team's L1 word making an L3 argument, and it is theirs to make.
- **L2 confirms, does not decide.** The checker's Return Type Rule relies on the rule (F-44, measured by `IncompatibleClassChangeError`); the team's JVM type mapping relies on it (`TypeMapping.tex:125`, Chase 2012, not cited by the exclusion notes); the prelude was flattened in 2009-2010 with no stated reason. These say the compiled path needs the rule; they do not say the language has it. The language's texts say that.
- **Where the entry misstates.** Its "Why" is L2→L1 and misdated: "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way" (2009 code, earlier than every text above; his phrase "the team's last record" was about the forest rule, rq 219), "and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper" (the paper keeps the rule and has no numbers and no tower; he was told on 09-24 that "the fact underneath it is narrower than you read it"). "He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen" joins the two meanings of specialisation and he said it was not an answer (rq 220). He was not shown the WD's "mutually exclusive" sentence when he chose (J0929 D4 found its absence from the brief), nor the right authors and dates (fixed 10-12). Both omissions understated the L1 case for the decision he took.
- **Default:** stands. The "Why" becomes the L1 grounds above, with the prelude's flat shape named as the team's compiled-world instance of the same answer and F-46 as the price of route C. The two sentences of rq 219 and 220 go to history. His (he held P-43 for his answer; one line to him).

### Tenet 6. The phase order (P-33). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason, L2 (a work plan).** The checker is the gate the compiled path runs first; code generation and the run time come after it; the natives are the switch-over's definition. The order was approved with phase 4 undesigned and its code-generation half unmeasured (W1 was launched after the yes). F-34 now measures that half at 52 walls.
- **Where the entry misstates.** "The interpreter's whole library" is wider than F-53's twelve, and his 10-26 goal says "the fuller library". No step names the bound flip (F-289). J1024 §6 already ruled the exit restated and two phase-4 zeros; I confirm. The 40 other components (F-290: 624 errors, 25 crashes) do not block the switch-over; they block P-12's step, so each reaches zero before that step or before the first program that needs it. That is the coordinator's view, his to confirm; it is sound.
- **Default:** phase 3 closes with 22c (ruling 5); P-33's phase 3 text restated as the thirteen under the compile command's own setting; phase 4 carries two zeros (the checker's and the code generator's over the thirteen); the 40 components placed before P-12's step. His (reads anew P-33's exit).

### Tenet 7. Unboxed doubles and `double[]` arrays (P-17, P-84). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason.** L1: the language's aim (`philosophy.tex`), value objects "an implementation may freely copy" (`objects.tex:38`), a `LinearSequence` of a value type "describes a sequence of 'unboxed' values" (`binary.tex:80`), Jan Maessen's note that the store under a sized array is what is unboxed (`future.tex:42`), the library's `nat` sizes on `Vector` and `Matrix`. ## 9. For Pavol

**What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. You named the bound as a possible linchpin, and you asked that the three layers be kept apart: what the Fortress language says; how the team built it on the Java virtual machine; and how Fortress meets Java.

**The verdict, first.**

- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.

**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.

- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
- The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.

**The compiler's small library, in plain words.** The team built two libraries: the interpreter's full one, and a small one for the compiler that they called "bogus", a "bogo-trait" and a "hopefully temporary hack". You decided the full one is the one library, and you asked whether we ported the small library's good designs back or just taught the checker to accept whatever the full library said.

Taken from the small library: the flat number types, the numeral type, ranges over 32-bit integers, each integer type's own `MIN` and `MAX`, the integer power, lazy comparison, and the rule that a component declares every member its interface marks abstract. Weighed and not taken, with the reason now dated: the small library's `fail` returning a declared bottom type (Steele, June 2011), which the team's own 2012 and 2019 texts later made unwritable; the small library's `comprises T` spelling of the self type (Steele, June 2012), whose fact the checker now reads from the bound, as Naden's last note pointed; and string concatenation with the string on the left only, which the specification's own rule contradicts.
- The rule for the future, which goes into the record: a design of the small library binds the full one when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A stub by the team's own words does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper.
- One place we had the full library's text against a backed design of the small one: the abstract members (row 816). You reversed that on 25 October. The sweep finds no other.

**The decisions to take, each with a default.**

1. **Close phase 3 with climb batch 22c.** Phase 3 is the work that made the type checker accept the full library's twelve core parts without error. Your framing is sound. The batch carries four rungs: the abstract-member repair you decided; the nine operator headers that differ between interface and component, with the export check made to read operators; the two library parts that `List` imports and the count never checked; and the one line that gives the compile command the `Any` bound, with ten test edits. Strike the sentence "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text" from P-26; the coordinator added it with no source. Default: strike. Move the two sentences of P-43's "Why" to history and write the language's grounds in their place. Default: yes.
5. **Say yes, informed, to the natives' form before batch 23.** A native is a library function whose body is Java. The decision keeps the library's own form, `builtinPrimitive("...")`, and changes only the string, to name a static Java method both paths can call. Ranking later consistent texts above an earlier self-contradicting one is the right rule for this language, as J0929 F3 said.
- **Where the entry misstates.** (a) Its reason is an L2 motive: the type group "worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible". A JVM limit the team hit is evidence about L2, not a reason to rank an L1 text. (b) Its list of the later word mixes layers and dates: "the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010" is L2 code, earlier than the WD's last edit (2010-12), earlier than the 2011 paper, with no stated reason (`6896886fb` is a code-generator commit whose message ends "this would be a good time to get coercion working"). ## 6. His framing of the phase (07:30:36)

This is the phase 3 exit review. So far the tenets hold. If the judgement holds them, no major re-evaluation of direction is needed; phase 3 closes with one more batch, **climb batch 22c** (or more if needed), for the rungs left, to exit phase 3 cleanly. Candidates: row 816's repair (P-158); the 9 operator headers that differ between api and component (row 782); `List`'s two unchecked imports (`CovariantCollection`, `OneShotFlag`); the bound `Any` for `fortress compile` (the probe's one small rung). Batch 23 (the natives) follows. This takes the place of ask 2's options (phase 3 done with its exit restated, or open until the wider zero); P-33's phase 3 text is rewritten after the judgement. The earlier asks 3 to 8 (P-58's informed yes; P-155 to cover the export check; P-75 withdrawn; his texts to correct; rq 35 and rq 230; batch 23's go) are still open, after the review.

## 7. The flat numbers: my framing corrected (07:46:17)

I had framed the judge's question as whether the prelude's flat numbers are a design of the language or a JVM measure. He corrected me: the record's digging decided the flat tower, and I was wrong. The grounds on record: the exclusion rule in the team's language texts (the 2011 paper, `exclusion.tick:141-152`; the 2012 Types chapter, `types.tick:355-376`; Naden 2012, "blanket … for the semantic benefits and the simplicity"; POPL 2019 keeps it); under the rule a nested tower is impossible (`ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, both `Integral` at different arguments); the Working Draft says the number types "are mutually exclusive" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`); Steele's 2016 talk shows a flat tower; the checker relies on the rule (F-44) and so does the JVM mapping (`TypeMapping.tex:125`); routes A, B and C weighed 09-22 to 09-24 (`reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md`, `reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md`, `reviews/mie-probes/`), A chosen 09-24; reviews D4 (09-29), the POPL recheck and V5 (10-23) keep it. What is open is narrower: P-43's stated reason, "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way", is the weakest ground and not his words (rq 219). The judge's real question for P-37: when does a design of the compiler's prelude bind the one library? My answer, for the judge to weigh: when the team's later word on the language backs it, as the exclusion rule backs the flat numbers.

## 8. The POSITIONS rewrites and the trap test (approved 07:42:15 and 07:48:49)
